title: Meat and milk (Exodus 23:19)
hook: "thou shalt not seethe a kid in its mother's milk" grew into separate dishes and waiting times

segments.voice: Yesterday, which animals: split hooves and chewing the cud, fins and scales. Your line was read the label.

Open the cabinets in a home that keeps kosher, and you might think they own twice the dishes they need. Two sets of plates, two sets of pots, two sets of silverware, sometimes with colored handles, red for one, blue for the other. Sometimes two sinks. Ask someone there if they want ice cream after a burger, and they might check the clock first. It all grows out of one short sentence in the Torah. A sentence about a baby goat.
screen: `TWO SETS OF DISHES.` → `RED HANDLES, BLUE HANDLES.` → `CHECKING THE CLOCK.`

segments.voice: "Thou shalt not seethe a kid in its mother's milk." Seethe means boil; a kid is a young goat. It's an oddly specific rule, and the Torah gives it not once but three times, twice in Exodus and once in Deuteronomy. The rabbis took that repetition seriously: three mentions, three prohibitions. Don't cook meat and milk together, don't eat them together, and don't benefit from the mixture, like selling it. Then they widened it, from a goat and its own mother's milk to any meat and any dairy. By rabbinic law, poultry counts as meat too. Fish and eggs are neither; they're called pareve, neutral, and can go with either. Pots and pans can absorb flavors, so kitchens keep separate dishes. And after eating meat, Jews who keep kosher wait before eating dairy. How long depends on family custom: some wait six hours, some three, some one, each handed down in different communities. All are respected traditions. Why this rule at all? The Torah doesn't say. Some commentators suggested it was to keep away from an ancient pagan practice. Others heard compassion in it: the milk meant to give a young animal life shouldn't be used to cook it. One puzzle the rabbis noticed: when Abraham hosts three visitors in Genesis, he serves them curd, milk and a calf, all at once. Different sages gave different answers to how that fits. They didn't hide the question.
screen: `A KID IN ITS MOTHER'S MILK.` · `THREE TIMES, THREE RULES.` · `SEPARATE DISHES, WAITING TIMES.` · `A PAGAN PRACTICE, OR COMPASSION?` · then, large: `SOME THINGS STAY APART.`

segments.voice: Picture your plate, empty, at the moment you'd reach for a second helping, and notice what the wanting feels like, right in the body. Then just wait. Not to punish yourself, but to see the space between one thing and the next.
Pareve, neutral foods like fish and eggs that count as neither meat nor dairy, and can be eaten with either under the kosher rule of meat and milk.
Your line: some things stay apart. Even in one kitchen. Day one hundred forty-six, done.

howItsDone: Jews who keep kosher don't cook or eat meat (including poultry) with dairy, keep separate dishes and utensils for each, and wait between meat and dairy according to family custom, often one, three or six hours.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Exodus 23:19b ('Thou shalt not seethe a kid in its mother's milk').
Poultry as rabbinic extension: Mishnah Chullin 8:1 and Chullin 104b (R. Akiva vs. R. Yose HaGelili). Confirm.
Waiting customs: six (many Eastern European), three (many German), one (Dutch). Generalizations; confirm.
Reasons: Maimonides (Guide 3:48) links it to idolatrous practice and also mentions it; compassion reading from other commentators (e.g. Ibn Ezra). Confirm attribution.
Abraham's meal (Genesis 18:8) and rabbinic answers mentioned without detail.
